[lehner-1985-hetepheres.md] Lehner argues that the shaft tomb G7000x east of the Great Pyramid, found by Reisner in 1925 with Hetepheres I's furniture, canopic chest and sealed but empty sarcophagus, was her original burial made under Khufu, and that Khufu later moved her body into the first of the queens' pyramids beside his own (G1-a) when it was built, leaving the shaft burial sealed. On this reading the empty sarcophagus was not the result of a robbery concealed from the king but of a reburial ordered by him.

[vyse-1840.md] Vyse blasted upward from Davison's Chamber in 1837 and opened four further relieving chambers above the King's Chamber (named for Wellington, Nelson, Lady Arbuthnot and Campbell), the topmost gabled. In these sealed chambers he found quarry marks in red ochre, including cartouches of Khufu and the names of work gangs. Some of the marks run under the joints between blocks, showing they were painted before the blocks were set. Vyse also had the pit in the floor of the Subterranean Chamber deepened to about 11 m and excavated beneath the coffer in the King's Chamber, finding solid masonry and rock in both cases. The lowest ceiling beams of the King's Chamber are cracked and had been plastered over in antiquity.

[cole-1925.md] source: Cole, J. H. (1925). Determination of the exact size and orientation of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Survey of Egypt Paper 39, Cairo.

[petrie-1883.md] Petrie's survey of the Great Pyramid gives the mean length of the base sides as 9068.8 inches (230.35 m), with the four sides differing by at most a few inches. The original height, reconstructed from the casing angle and the base, is 5776 inches ± 7 (146.71 m). The casing angle is 51° 52' ± 2'. The sides are oriented to true north within about 3 to 4 arcminutes.

[edgar-1910.md] The Grotto is a natural cavity or fissure in the rock uncovered when the builders levelled the site; the well shaft passes through it, and the builders walled it with small courses of stone and packed it with sand and gravel as foundation fill. Investigators after Al Mamoun's time broke through the lower courses of its south wall, found only sand and gravel, and threw their spoil down the well, blocking its lower end. Wedged at the east edge of the deep hollow in the Grotto's floor lies a large granite stone of broken appearance, apparently a fragment of a larger block, with two worked surfaces at right angles to each other and parts of two large holes drilled through it.

[edgar-1910.md] The large granite block found by Professor Flinders Petrie in the Descending Passage has a four-inch drill hole through it; the two next largest granite pieces also each have a pair of drill holes. The block lacks the projections and rebates of the Granite Leaf; Petrie's suggestion that it was a further portcullis from the Antechamber faces the objection that the grooves there are too wide. Its original purpose is unknown.

[finds-list.md] Great Pyramid of Khufu: granite sarcophagus in the King's Chamber, lid missing; chamber walls undecorated; in the Queen's Chamber air shafts, a diorite ball, a copper hook and a cedar plank (the Dixon relics, 1872); hieroglyphic graffiti including Khufu's name in the relieving chambers; no human remains recorded.

The Queen's Chamber lies on the pyramid's central axis and has a corbelled niche in its east wall. The Grand Gallery is 47 m long and 8.6 m high. The chamber floors lie at roughly 43 m (King's) and 21 m (Queen's) above the base.

[reisner-1927-hetepheres.md] Reisner reports the discovery in 1925 of a 30 m shaft (G7000x) east of the Great Pyramid containing the gilded furniture, inlaid boxes, canopic chest with preserved organs in natron solution, and the alabaster sarcophagus of Queen Hetepheres I, wife of Snefru and mother of Khufu. The sarcophagus was sealed and intact but, when opened, empty. Seal impressions in the deposit carry Khufu's name. Reisner proposed that her original tomb at Dahshur had been robbed and the body lost, and that officials reburied the surviving equipment at Giza without informing the king.

[scanpyramids-2017.md] Three independent muon detection techniques (nuclear emulsion films placed in the Queen's Chamber, scintillator hodoscopes in the Queen's Chamber, and gas detectors outside the pyramid) detected a large void above the Grand Gallery. The void is at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to that of the Grand Gallery (about 8 m high), located between 50 and 70 m above ground. Its muon signal is comparable to that of the Grand Gallery, consistent with an empty (air-filled) space. Muon imaging records only material above the detector positions; the bedrock beneath the pyramid is outside the method's view from these positions. [scanpyramids-2017.md] Three independent muon detection techniques (nuclear emulsion films placed in the Queen's Chamber, scintillator hodoscopes in the Queen's Chamber, and gas detectors outside the pyramid) detected a large void above the Grand Gallery. The void is at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to that of the Grand Gallery (about 8 m high), located between 50 and 70 m above ground. Its muon signal is comparable to that of the Grand Gallery, consistent with an empty (air-filled) space. Muon imaging records only material above the detector positions; the bedrock beneath the pyramid is outside the method's view from these positions. A later campaign (2023) confirmed the void and imaged a 9 m corridor behind the north face chevrons.

[edgar-1910.md] The Grotto is a natural cavity or fissure in the rock uncovered when the builders levelled the site; the well shaft passes through it, and the builders walled it with small courses of stone and packed it with sand and gravel as foundation fill. Investigators after Al Mamoun's time broke through the lower courses of its south wall, found only sand and gravel, and threw their spoil down the well, blocking its lower end. Wedged at the east edge of the deep hollow in the Grotto's floor lies a large granite stone of broken appearance, apparently a fragment of a larger block, with two worked surfaces at right angles to each other and parts of two large holes drilled through it.

[lehner-1997.md] Great Pyramid of Khufu: base 230.33 m, original height 146.59 m, slope 51° 50' 40". Volume about 2.6 million cubic metres; roughly 2.3 million blocks. The King's Chamber, lined and roofed in granite, measures about 10.47 m by 5.23 m and is 5.84 m high; above it are five relieving chambers roofed with granite beams, the topmost gabled. The Queen's Chamber lies on the pyramid's central axis and has a corbelled niche in its east wall. The Grand Gallery is 47 m long and 8.6 m high. The chamber floors lie at roughly 43 m (King's) and 21 m (Queen's) above the base.

[vyse-1840.md] Vyse blasted upward from Davison's Chamber in 1837 and opened four further relieving chambers above the King's Chamber (named for Wellington, Nelson, Lady Arbuthnot and Campbell), the topmost gabled. In these sealed chambers he found quarry marks in red ochre, including cartouches of Khufu and the names of work gangs. Some of the marks run under the joints between blocks, showing they were painted before the blocks were set. Vyse also had the pit in the floor of the Subterranean Chamber deepened to about 11 m and excavated beneath the coffer in the King's Chamber, finding solid masonry and rock in both cases. The lowest ceiling beams of the King's Chamber are cracked and had been plastered over in antiquity.

[cole-1925.md] source: Cole, J. H. (1925). Determination of the exact size and orientation of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Survey of Egypt Paper 39, Cairo.

[lehner-1985-hetepheres.md] Lehner argues that the shaft tomb G7000x east of the Great Pyramid, found by Reisner in 1925 with Hetepheres I's furniture, canopic chest and sealed but empty sarcophagus, was her original burial made under Khufu, and that Khufu later moved her body into the first of the queens' pyramids beside his own (G1-a) when it was built, leaving the shaft burial sealed. On this reading the empty sarcophagus was not the result of a robbery concealed from the king but of a reburial ordered by him.

[edgar-1910.md] The large granite block found by Professor Flinders Petrie in the Descending Passage has a four-inch drill hole through it; the two next largest granite pieces also each have a pair of drill holes. The block lacks the projections and rebates of the Granite Leaf; Petrie's suggestion that it was a further portcullis from the Antechamber faces the objection that the grooves there are too wide. Its original purpose is unknown.
